newsitem.title: UK: UK wage floor may hit jobs/industry relations.
newsitem.headline: UK wage floor may hit jobs/industry relations.

text.p: A minimum wage set at too high a level could return Britain to the days of regular strikes as well as costing thousands of jobs, employers group the Institute of Directors (IOD) said on Monday.

The country's largest union UNISON, which represents 1.3 million public sector workers, said it would be asking the new Labour government to deliver a minimum wage of half the median male salary, or 4.42 per hour on updated on figures.
"This will be very bad news and really hit a lot of people," said Ruth Lea, head of the IOD's policy unit.
"In certain companies and certain industrial sectors -- for instance textiles and security -- even a minimum wage of 4.0 pounds could simply mean firms say "we shut our doors," Lea said.

The National Union of Knitwear, footwear and allied trades (NUKAFT) whose members tend to be amongst the higher paid workers in the sector, with male average earnings of around 6.0 stg per hour and female of some 4.64, has declined to put a figure on the level of the minimum wage.
"We'll be putting forward recommendations to the Low Pay Commission but it's really up to them to decide the level," a NUKAFT spokesman said.
"The question is really what's best for the country as a whole and...the people who are most likely to benefit are those who work for companies that aren't unionised."

The Trades Union Congress's (TUC) official policy on the minimum wage is similarly non-prescriptive. "The TUC's keeping its option open so it can play a constructive part in the Low Pay Commission," a TUC spokesman said.

last year's annual TUC conference passed a motion calling for 4.26 stg per hour -- half the then median male salary -- but it also carried a general council statement which left the question open. The general council statement takes precedence.

The IOD's Lea argues that the minimum wage will mean that Britain's recent good performance in industrial relations will be jeopardised as workers struggle to maintain pay differentials. "Industrial differentials are hotly fought for -- think of the potential for industrial disputes," she said.

The Confederation of British industry has said the employment consequences of a minimum wage increase as the rate at which it is set moves above 3.0 stg, whilst the British Chambers of Commerce argues that at 3.50 an hour 15 percent of small firms are affected, while 4.25 would catch 55 percent in the net.

A UNISON spokeswoman estimated some 26 percent of the workforce would benefit from a minimum wage of 4.42 compared with 24 percent that would benefit from a rate of 4.26 stg -- a figure based on last year's median pay.
UNISON also attaches little credence to the argument that other workers would try to maintain differentials.
Frank Wilkinson, Senior Research officer in the Centre for Business Research at Cambridge University's applied economics department takes a similar view.
"I can't find any substantial evidence that people at the top use the lower salaries of the lower paid when they are arguing about their own pay," he said.
"Skilled workers tend to use occupations very close to them or higher up," he said.
Moreover, he argues the long-term benefits of a minimum wage in terms of producing a highly motivated, more productive workforce will outweigh the short term negative impact of any job losses.
"If you want to develop a high-performance economy where service and quality improves at every level then that is an argument for a higher minimum wage," he added.
"The current position helps employers who are themselves inefficient rather than the workers. We've had long periods of high unemployment and that has caused the value of workers to sink," he said.
Last week, the Labour government announced plans for a Low Pay Commission to take evidence from employers and workers' representatives before recommending a new minimum wage.
